units.label: HPSG语法分布、相似度及多样性比较
units.description: 复用既有六LLM及人类NYT文本，加入WSJ/Wikipedia，以ERG解析计数和语料级统计比较。

units.label: 个人作者变异
units.description: 复用NYT中12位超过100句作者，与六模型的归一化类型向量作配对比较和平衡抽样检查。

units.label: 显著/长尾构式与词条示例分析
units.description: 复用解析结果，通过独有频繁词条、长尾构式和语法层级解释差异；不新增生成实验。

facts.statement: 以HPSG正式句法理论的ERG实现比较LLM生成与人类NYT风格新闻的语法足迹，分析句法构式、词汇类型、形态规则及词条使用；不训练文本来源分类器。
复用Muñoz-Ortiz等2024数据：人类NYT导语来自2023-10-01至2024-01-24 Archive API；六模型以标题+导语前3词生成文本，LLaMA7/13/30/65B、Falcon7B、Mistral7B均早于2023-10-01发布。

method_function.text: 记录既有生成任务/输入和时间关系。

facts.statement: 表1句数分别为LLaMA7/13/30/65B 37825/37800/37568/38107，Falcon27769，Mistral35086，人类NYT26102；另用Redwoods WSJ43043句及Wikipedia10726句作不同风格/体裁人类对照。

method_function.text: 区分源数据规模与后续25K抽样。

facts.statement: 采用ERG2025版本、ACE（脚注下载0.9.34）、PyDelphin及NumPy/Pandas/scikit-learn解析/统计derivation，分别计短语构式、词汇屈折/派生规则、词汇类型及词条频数。

method_function.text: 明确实际解析工具与语义类别。

facts.statement: 将构式/类型频次按总出现数归一化成向量，比较cosine；句法、词汇类型、词汇规则分别分析，个体比较另合并全部HPSG类型。PCA仅用于放大98–100%相似范围的可视化，附录B表8–10给原始cosine。

method_function.text: 提清相似度输入、分母和投影用途。

facts.statement: 作者以新于模型发布的新闻降低训练见过对应文章风险；同数据允许对照前人UD结果；WSJ同新闻不同风格、Wikipedia不同体裁检验模式是否跨风格/体裁。

method_function.text: 分开时间设计、分析框架对照和跨语料对照。

facts.statement: 使用Shannon entropy H和Gini–Simpson 1−λ；前者衡量均匀性，后者为随机两token不同type概率。附录C以10000次置换比较原始人类与合并LLM，除lexical-rule Simpson p=.13外均p<.01。

method_function.text: 区分多样性统计的对象及例外。

facts.statement: 逐类型相对频率比较采用Mann–Whitney U，附录D列未校正p≤.05的句法/词汇类型/规则，频繁与低频分开；作者明确多重比较FDR后均不再低于.05，仅9个数据集。

method_function.text: 保留探索性筛选及校正结论。

facts.statement: 语料级句法/词汇type分布的模型彼此紧密聚集；人类NYT更近WSJ而非Wikipedia；Falcon是lexical-type/规则较突出例外，NYT人与多数模型形态规则分布则很近。

method_function.text: 反映分层结果而非笼统语法全异。

facts.statement: 句法构式Shannon人类3.342高于各模型3.221–3.284，合并LLM3.265；词汇type方向相反，Falcon4.700低于人类4.727，而其余模型更高（LLaMA13B4.877）。

method_function.text: 报告多样性层次反转与模型例外。

facts.statement: 挑NYT中12位各有>100句作者，以归一化构式/type向量cosine比较人-人、人-LLM、LLM-LLM；因模型文本更多，另从模型随机抽取平衡样本检查分布相似。

method_function.text: 说明个体作者选择、配对层次及辅助平衡控制。

facts.statement: 作者报告人-人相似度较人-LLM低，LLM-LLM最紧密；词汇type个人差异尤其大。将LLM称为人类语法的平均化表现是解释，非直接观测内部平均机制。

method_function.text: 区分配对结果与平均化叙事。

facts.statement: 长尾筛选为同量NYT样本中人类出现0或1次、LLM样本>10次的构式，如数字串、词汇连词片段、括号修饰、mass noun coordination及measure noun修饰；作者强调人类缺例可能仅抽样偶然。

method_function.text: 记录长尾选择阈值和证据限制。

facts.statement: 表3与表4注明25K（表4明确25K句）抽样；独有词条/type按样本有无比较，表5人类top15、表6特指LLaMA65B，不是所有模型合并；同一表3all llms为池化抽样对照。

method_function.text: 厘清样本、池化和模型专属表。

facts.statement: 样本中人类更常用若干低频风格构式（如participial clause表4 1736 vs模型均1116），LLM较多一般head-complement（164806 vs224529）及问句/数量短语；后续head-complement内部子结构分析未实施。

method_function.text: 将举例绝对出现数与相对检验区分。

facts.statement: 用ERG词汇层级区分同表面词的句法用法，例如law_n2可接从句、law_n1 mass-count；本文样本人类出现前者、模型仅后者。以高频但一方独有条目作定性例证，低频小类不轻作解释。

method_function.text: 保留类型/词条/词形的实质关系。

facts.statement: 正文称Shannon与Simpson排序相同，但附录图10实际有次序变化：句法中合并LLM与LLaMA13B交换、词汇type13B与7B等次序也不同；共同宏观趋势不等于完全同排名。

method_function.text: 保留可视复核的来源不一致。

facts.statement: 论文只对英语/主要NYT风格作具体例证；ERG一般94%覆盖取自版本文档，不是本文逐模型成功率。全文未完整报告解析失败处置、歧义最佳树选择、分句/截断、25K及池化抽样方法/次数/种子、生成温度/全文提示、置换单位与FDR变体。

method_function.text: 说明已核未报告和一般覆盖与实际分母区别。

This study provides the first comprehensive
comparison of New York Times-style text generated by six large language models against
real, human-authored NYT writing. The comparison is based on a formal syntactic theory.
We use Head-driven Phrase Structure Grammar
(HPSG) to analyze the grammatical structure
of the texts. We then investigate and illustrate
the differences in the distributions of HPSG
grammar types, revealing systematic distinctions between human and LLM-generated writing. These findings contribute to a deeper understanding of the syntactic behavior of LLMs
as well as humans, within the NYT genre.

Our study is concerned with the analysis of the
grammatical properties of LLM-generated texts as
compared to human-authored texts. Here, we review the literature with a similar focus. This leaves
out of scope papers concerned with building classifiers or with sentiment and semantic analysis.

We find that human authors and LLMs clearly differ
in terms of their corresponding syntactic and lexical
type distributions, and that this may persist across
style and genre.11 If we consider only syntactic and
lexical types (Figures 2-3),12 we see clearly that
human-authored texts are distinct in their HPSG
type distributions from the closely-clustered LLMs
and furthermore, that human-authored NYT texts
are more similar to WSJ (different style, same
genre) than to Wikipedia (different genre). This is
true for syntactic and lexical types, although with
lexical types, Falcon is an outlier, and the effect of
style and genre seems bigger. However, in terms
of lexical (inflectional and derivational) rules, we
observe that the distribution of human NYT authors is very similar to LLMs except Falcon. These
findings align with what we see when we apply
diversity metrics (§5.2). In this paper, we focus
on the most salient differences between LLMs and
human NYT authors, and investigating the intriguing role of lexical rules remains future work. One
hypothesis is that the distribution of lexical rules
is very closely tied to genre and style (and that the
Falcon model is somehow special in this respect).

5.2 Diversity
To quantify diversity in the texts we applied two
biodiversity measures that have become standard in
stylometry and authorship attribution (McKinney,
2010; Stamatatos, 2009): Shannon entropy H
and the Gini–Simpson index 1 − λ. The former
captures the balance (evenness) of the distribution,
while the latter is interpretable as the probability
that two randomly drawn tokens belong to different
types. Because both indices give the same rank
orderings in our data (see Appendix C), we only
discuss Shannon entropy here.

C

Diversity Measures

Figure 10 shows the diversities of constructions,
lexical types and lexical rules measured with both
the Shannon Index (on the left) and Simpson Index
(on the right), as discussed in Section 5.2. Scores
for the original human-generated sentences are
shown with a star (⋆), LLMs with a dot (•) and
the combined LLMs with a larger dot (•)
We measured the significance of the difference
between the original human-generated sentences
and combined LLM sentences using a permutation
test, sampled 10,000 times. All combinations had
an observed p-value of less than 0.01, except for the
Lexical Rules measured with the Simpson Index
(which is less sensitive to outliers), with p = 0.13.

As far as we know, our study is the first pairwise
comparison of human authors and LLMs along
detailed grammatical dimensions, and we show for
the first time that a human-authored text is more
similar to an LLM-generated text than to another
human-authored text (by a different author). This
makes sense if we see an LLM-generated text as
“averaged” with respect to grammatical features that
humans use in their language. This can also be seen
in their increased use of the most general structures
such as the head-complement phrase (Figure 5).
Our results also confirm the previous observations
that LLMs are very similar to each other in terms
of the types of constructions that they use (see §2).

5.1.2 Syntactic long tail
It is possible that some salient differences lie in the
“long tail” of the distributions (not shown in Figure
5). The ERG is a unique resource to study this
long tail, being a comprehensive representation
of the English language which, while validated
empirically, was developed with close attention
to a wide range of phenomena, not only the most
frequently occurring ones.
The following constructions occur only 0 or 1
times in a sample from human-authored NYT text,
while similar size samples from the LLM-generated
texts contain more than 10 instances: sequence of
numbers; fragment lexical conjunction (“But!”);
parenthetical modifier (“Some person (tall) was
running away”); mass noun coordination (‘sand
and gravel’);14 modifier phrase formed from ‘mea-

sure’ nouns (We slept the last mile).
Humans use all of these long-tail constructions
occasionally (which is how they came to be represented in the ERG in the first place); their not occurring in the NYT dataset could just be by chance.
Future experiments with more data are needed. In
the meantime, we show that HPSG analysis aligns
with previous findings with UD (e.g. that current
LLMs are known to favor numbers and measurerelated vocabulary (Muñoz-Ortiz et al., 2024)), and
identify constructions possibly typical for LLMs
which have not previously been noted (§6.1).

of the text. We note also the words ‘fact’ and ‘clear’
as generic but persuasive, and as such perhaps typical for LLM language (Table 6).

5.2 Diversity
To quantify diversity in the texts we applied two
biodiversity measures that have become standard in
stylometry and authorship attribution (McKinney,
2010; Stamatatos, 2009): Shannon entropy H
and the Gini–Simpson index 1 − λ. The former
captures the balance (evenness) of the distribution,
while the latter is interpretable as the probability
that two randomly drawn tokens belong to different
types. Because both indices give the same rank
orderings in our data (see Appendix C), we only
discuss Shannon entropy here.

Limitations
There are many methodological limitations related
to work with LLM-generated text. An LLM will
generate a different text every time, and a lot depends on the prompt, and our resources in terms of
generation are limited. Otherwise the main limitation here is that we only look at one genre (NYTstyle news). We do include other types of data and
our analysis of the overall distribution reflects this;
however in our discussion of specific examples we
still focus on the NYT-style data. Another limitation is that we only have large HPSG grammars for
a handful of languages, and indeed only the ERG
is big enough to cover 94% of news text, limiting
the utility of our approach in comparisons of text
in other languages. This is why our study is only
about English.

The English Resource grammar is a grammar of
English implemented in HPSG (Flickinger, 2000,
2011).2 The ERG is continuously developed as
part of the DELPH-IN open-source grammar engineering initiative.3 It is a broad coverage precision
grammar, meaning that it will parse 94%4 of reasonably well-edited English text but is not expected
to yield any structure for a sentence impossible in
English. Since the grammar is precise and consistent, it can be used to automatically create precise
and consistent treebanks. It has been shown that
including such treebanks in the training data improves performance of various NLP systems (Lin
et al., 2022; Hajdik et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2018;

The ‘NYT’ datasets from Muñoz-Ortiz et al.
2024 include the original New York Times (NYT)
article lead paragraphs and LLM-generated texts
obtained from 6 different LLMs by prompting them
with the headlines together with the first 3 words
of the lead paragraph.9 The original NYT humanauthored data consists of the lead paragraphs for
articles between October 1, 2023, and January 24,
2024 obtained with the NYT Archive API.10 The
LLMs they used were all released prior to October
1, 2023, and included various versions of LLaMA
(Touvron et al., 2023), the 7B version of Falcon (Almazrouei et al., 2023), and the 7B version of Mistral (Jiang et al., 2023). Following Muñoz-Ortiz
et al. (2024), we want to consider the influence of
scaling (different LLaMas with the same architecture, training dataset and training setup, but different model size) separately from the other aspects
that differentiate the LLMs (LLaMa vs Mistral vs
